title: Mid-Point Adjustments Can Be the Winning Strategy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues for building in a deliberate mid-point review into any strategy or initiative, using research from professors Jonah Berger and Devin Pope on over 18,000 NBA games to make the case. Their surprising finding -- that teams trailing slightly at halftime actually won more often -- is attributed to the adjustments teams make when they realize their original plan isn't working, adjustments they likely wouldn't make while comfortably ahead. The essay extends this into a general leadership framework: revisit assumptions, reassess key contributors' roles, and account for what's changed in the environment, all at the midpoint rather than waiting until the end.
points: Professors Jonah Berger and Devin Pope studied over 18,000 NBA games and found teams trailing slightly at halftime won more often overall.
The likely explanation: trailing teams make strategic adjustments at the midpoint that leading teams don't bother making.
A good mid-point review involves revisiting the assumptions behind the original strategy that have turned out to be false.
It's also worth reassessing whether key contributors are performing as expected -- sometimes a role change, not a replacement, is the fix.
Leaders should account for what's changed in the competitive or market environment since the initiative began, not just at launch.
quotes: Smart leaders course-correct when they need to. They aren't bashful to admit that the initial strategy isn't working perfectly and that they need to make adjustments mid-stream.
The duo examined more than 18,000 NBA games and found something startling. Namely, that trailing slightly at half-time led to a significant increase in winning percentage.
Teams likely made adjustments at half-time they probably wouldn't have made had they been leading in the game.
Leaders who stick with their top performers no matter what the evidence is often go down in flames with them.
Short-term adjustments are the key to long-term success. Even small or tiny adjustments can affect the outcome.
All initiatives, projects, and games are metaphorically played on a sailboat. Adjust those sails for the wind.
